Self-employed cash planning: an invoice is not take-home income

Four charts connect invoices, operating costs, collection delays, owner withdrawals and a separate hypothetical tax earmark.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore invoices, operating cash and an earmark for taxes

Interactive planning lab

Invoiced operating profit before owner draws$100,800
Year-end tax earmark target$25,200
Additional starting cash needed$7,300

Hypothetical twelve-month cash ledger with equal invoices each month and no opening receivables or payables. Operating cash costs and owner withdrawals occur at each month’s start; invoice m is collected at the end of month m + delay. Only receipts inside twelve months are counted; later invoices remain receivable. Positive invoice-based operating profit creates a month-end tax earmark even before collection. This percentage is a planning allowance, not actual tax or CPP/QPP. Earmark is held, with no remittance modeled; if cash is insufficient it is an unfunded target, not a funded account. Free cash deducts the target once. No corporate salary/dividend rules, GST/HST, deductible-expense assessment, depreciation, bad debt, financing cost or tax deadline is calculated. Negative points are unfunded needs, not an approved overdraft.

The central idea

Build the household draw from cash that remains after business obligations and a tax provision. Profit, collected cash and uncommitted cash answer different questions.

01

Keep invoices, operating profit, cash and owner draws distinct

A customer invoice can record work completed without putting money into the bank. Operating profit can be positive while cash is tied up in receivables. An owner’s withdrawal then moves cash into the household budget without changing the modeled operating profit.

The CRA’s sole-proprietorship overview explains that personal income tax applies to business net income and that instalment payments may be required. It does not make a fixed percentage of every invoice a universal tax rate.

This tool is a simplified management ledger for an unincorporated owner, rather than a tax return. All invoices exclude sales taxes. Costs are assumed to be operating cash payments; the model does not determine whether an expense is deductible or account for inventory, capital allowances or GST/HST.

02

Follow the same twelve-month example through the ledger

The default issues CAD 12,000 of invoices each month, or CAD 144,000 over twelve months. Operating cash costs are 30% of invoiced revenue: CAD 3,600 a month and CAD 43,200 for the year.

Invoice-based operating profit is CAD 100,800 before owner draws and the tax provision. The owner withdraws CAD 4,000 at each month’s start, totaling CAD 48,000. Those withdrawals reduce the business cash available even though they do not reduce this operating-profit figure.

A hypothetical 25% allowance on positive operating profit creates a CAD 2,100 monthly tax earmark, reaching CAD 25,200. This is a target reserved for future obligations, not an assessment of income tax, CPP or QPP. A loss creates no new earmark in the illustration and no assumed tax refund.

03

Allow for the collection delay and opening cash needs

With one full month of collection delay, month one’s invoice is received at the end of month two. The schedule starts without older invoices waiting to be collected. Consequently, only eleven monthly invoices arrive inside the twelve-month horizon.

Cash receipts are CAD 132,000 and CAD 12,000 remains receivable at year-end. The final invoice is not written off; its later receipt simply lies outside this chart. Operating costs and household withdrawals are still paid in month twelve.

Starting cash is CAD 10,000. At the start of month two, the second CAD 7,600 of operating costs and owner draws falls due before any customer receipt. With the first month’s CAD 2,100 earmark also reserved, uncommitted cash is negative CAD 7,300. The model therefore needs CAD 17,300 at the start, or CAD 7,300 beyond the selected amount.

04

Do not treat earmarked money as spare household income

The year-end cash ledger before the earmark is CAD 50,800: opening cash plus receipts, less operating costs and withdrawals. Subtracting the CAD 25,200 target leaves CAD 25,600 uncommitted. The waterfall reconciles that amount from invoices by also removing the uncollected balance.

The earmark remains cash if it has been funded and held. Subtract it once when measuring spendable resources. If cash is below the target, the target is partly unfunded; recording a reserve label does not create the missing money.

No remittance is made inside this model. If a fully funded earmark is later used for an equal tax payment, both cash and the outstanding earmark fall by that amount, leaving uncommitted cash unchanged at that instant. Actual payment dates and revised amounts still need a separate calendar.

05

Test customer timing and owner withdrawals together

The collection-delay bars keep the invoice and expense assumptions fixed while changing when customers pay. Even zero full-month delay requires opening cash here because costs and draws precede month-end receipts.

The matrix changes owner withdrawals and the hypothetical earmark percentage. It measures additional opening cash, rather than recommending a draw or claiming that a selected percentage settles the tax bill. More available opening cash can bridge timing; it does not make an ongoing loss sustainable.

Replace the equal invoices with a detailed forecast before using a real plan. Review collection risk, expense due dates, tax estimates and remittances, then pass the household only the net amount it can use. The existing variable-income guide begins at that household stage; this guide explains the business cash steps that come first.
